scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Users on pc_0_0 (10.0.0.2) and pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2) report they cannot
reach each other in either direction. Both hosts can still ping their
own gateways (10.0.0.1 and 10.0.1.1). The NOC insists the fabric is
healthy: every BGP session is Established, all routes are present on
every router, no interface has flapped, and all FRR daemons are
running. Identify what is silently eating the traffic.

injection.action: add a FORWARD DROP rule for pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 transit

post_inject_check.expect: 0% loss   (gateway still OK -- INPUT chain untouched)

scenario.ground_truth:
Affected component: leaf_router_0_0 iptables FORWARD chain
Mechanism: a DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 discards every forwarded
  packet with source in 10.0.0.0/24 and destination in 10.0.1.0/24.
  All pc_0_0 traffic must transit leaf_router_0_0 (its only gateway),
  so pc_0_0 -> pc_0_1 packets die there. The reverse direction fails
  too, despite matching no rule on its way in: pc_0_1's echo requests
  ARE delivered to pc_0_0, but pc_0_0's replies (src 10.0.0.2, dst
  10.0.1.2) match the rule and are dropped -- a one-directional filter
  breaks bidirectional traffic. Routing and BGP are completely
  healthy; the drop is at the firewall layer. Local delivery to the
  gateway itself uses the INPUT chain, which is untouched, so both
  hosts still ping their gateways.
Localization: leaf_router_0_0
Root cause: extraneous iptables FORWARD DROP rule
  (-s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24) on leaf_router_0_0
Fix: `iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP` on
  leaf_router_0_0
scenario.fix_spec:
remove the DROP rule on leaf_router_0_0 --
`iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP`

agent.diagnosis_text:
A Linux netfilter (iptables) DROP rule silently discards all inter-host
traffic at leaf_router_0_0. The rule, present only in the live kernel and
absent from any on-disk ruleset, is:

  -A FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP

It sits in the filter/FORWARD chain, which the kernel traverses for every
packet being routed through (not destined to) the box. When pc_0_0
(10.0.0.2) tries to reach pc_0_1 (10.0.1.2), the ICMP echo request
arrives at leaf_router_0_0, matches the rule source/destination, and is
discarded without generating any ICMP Unreachable — explaining the
complete timeout. The reverse direction also fails because pc_0_0's echo
replies (src=10.0.0.2, dst=10.0.1.2) pass through the same FORWARD chain
on leaf_router_0_0 and match the same rule, so pc_0_1 never receives an
answer either. Because iptables operates beneath FRR, the routing table,
BGP sessions, and interface state are all genuinely healthy — exactly why
the NOC's control-plane checks showed nothing wrong. The hit counter
(12 packets / 1008 bytes) confirms active drops. The rule was injected at
runtime (no /etc/iptables/rules.v4 exists), so it will survive FRR restarts
but not a container restart.

Root cause: A rogue iptables FORWARD DROP rule was dynamically injected
into leaf_router_0_0 blocking all traffic from 10.0.0.0/24 to 10.0.1.0/24.

Corrective fix: On leaf_router_0_0, run:
  iptables -D FORWARD -s 10.0.0.0/24 -d 10.0.1.0/24 -j DROP
This immediately restores end-to-end reachability. To prevent recurrence,
ensure iptables state is persisted via /etc/iptables/rules.v4 and any
startup scripts are audited for unauthorised rule injection.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly names leaf_router_0_0 as the affected device multiple times.

per_axis.axis: must-recognize-filter-pattern: recognizes healthy routing + healthy BGP with silent forwarding loss as a packet-filter fault, not a routing fault
per_axis.rationale: The agent explicitly states routing/BGP are healthy and attributes the connectivity loss to an iptables FORWARD DROP rule blocking transit packets, matching the expected packet-filter diagnosis.

per_axis.axis: bonus-explains-asymmetric-drop: explains that the single directional rule (10.0.0.0/24 -> 10.0.1.0/24) also kills the reverse ping because replies match it

Recommends deleting the exact FORWARD DROP rule with iptables -D which directly restores connectivity and adds sensible persistence/audit advice.

The investigation log contains direct evidence (iptables-save showing the FORWARD DROP rule, ping timeouts, ip_forward=1, host routes) and the agent's inferences follow logically; minor claims (rules.v4 absence and packet hit counter) are implied by truncated outputs but overall the conclusion is well-supported.
